title: What blood pressure numbers mean
examples: Why does blood pressure have two numbers?

explain.say: Blood pressure is how hard blood pushes on the walls of your arteries. It rises and falls with every heartbeat, like a wave.
When the left ventricle squeezes, it pushes a gush of blood into the arteries and the pressure peaks. That top number is the systolic pressure.
Between beats the heart relaxes, but the stretchy artery walls spring back and keep pushing, so pressure falls but never to zero. That lowest number is the diastolic pressure.
So a reading like 120 over 80 means the push peaks at 120 and drops to 80 between beats. The units are millimetres of mercury, from the old mercury gauges.

faq.a: Systolic pressure is the highest pressure in your arteries, reached when the heart squeezes and pushes blood out. It is the top number in a reading.
asks: What is the top number in blood pressure?
Tell me about the squeeze: systolic

faq.a: Diastolic pressure is the lowest pressure in your arteries, between beats while the heart relaxes and refills. Stretchy artery walls keep it from falling to zero. It is the bottom number.
asks: What is the bottom number in blood pressure?
Tell me about the rest: diastolic

faq.a: It means the pressure in the artery peaks at 120 millimetres of mercury when the heart beats, and falls to 80 between beats. It is a typical value for a resting young adult.
asks: What do the two blood pressure numbers mean?

faq.q: Why is it measured in millimetres of mercury?
faq.a: Early gauges used a tube of mercury, and the pressure was read as how many millimetres high it pushed the mercury. The unit stayed even though most gauges are now electronic.

faq.q: Why does blood pressure change during the day?
faq.a: Your body adjusts it all the time. Exercise, excitement and standing up raise the heart rate or squeeze blood vessels, and rest or sleep lowers it.
asks: Does blood pressure go up when you exercise?

facts: Blood pressure is written as systolic over diastolic, in millimetres of mercury (mmHg).
Elastic artery walls stretch when the heart beats and recoil between beats, keeping blood moving.
